```{r}
#| label: setup
#| output: false

library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(sf)

epsg_wgs_84 <- 4326 # WGS 84
epsg_nl <- 28992    # Amersfoort / RD New

# set European format for graphs
scales::number_options(
  decimal.mark = ",",
  big.mark = ".",
  currency.prefix = "€"
)

theme_update(text = element_text(family = "Atlas Grotesk")) # house style
```

```{r}
#| label: import-data
#| cache: true
#| output: false

lisa <- read_sf("data/lisa2017.parquet") # internal

gwl  <- read_sf("data/GWL.gpkg") |> # internal
  remove_empty(which = c("rows", "cols")) |>
  remove_constant() |>
  mutate(oid = row_number(), .before = everything())

# from https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/dossier/nederland-regionaal/geografische-data/gegevens-per-postcode
bevolking_pc6 <- read_sf("data/cbs_pc6_2025_v1.gpkg") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~replace_values(.x, c(-99997, -99995) ~ NA))) |>
  remove_empty("cols")

nl_border <- read_sf("data/landsgrens.geojson") # internal, 2023
```


## Introduction

The Netherlands is planning to address the housing crisis
by building new housing, with concentrations in several large-scale locations.
These grootschalige woningbouwlocaties must have access to jobs and amenities
by sustainable modes of transport—public transport, bicycle, and foot—
to ensure that they are both sustainable and livable.

In this analysis, we seek to develop
a meaningful measure of the **bicycle accessibility**
of the grootschalige woningbouwlocaties.
This is a difficult task because of their large-scale nature—
as these locations are often whole new urban districts
with associated new street infrastructure, amenities, and even jobs,
assessments of existing cycling infrastructure give an incomplete picture.

Therefore, we choose to focus our analysis on **job accessibility**,
as employment opportunities and locations are less likely to change
with the development of new housing,
when compared with street infrastructure itself
or amenities within neighborhoods.

As a rudimentary approach,
we can consider the number of jobs
available within cycling distance of the new housing areas
and make comparisons between them.

A more advanced analysis
could distribute hypothetical new citizens across these housing areas
and calculate job accessibility metrics for them on an individual basis.

## Existing jobs within cycling distance

In the Netherlands,
city planners [typically use](https://www.mrdh.nl/interview/potentie-fiets-woon-werkverkeer)
7,5 km as the maximum distance cycled to work, with 15 km for e-bikes.
We can therefore take a 7,5 km buffer around the large-scale housing areas
as a very rough estimate of the bike-accessible employment area.[^fiets-1]

[^fiets-1]: The actual area is smaller,
because it would reflect network distance rather than crow-flies distance
and account for the fact that not all residents live on the edge of the area.

We then count the number of jobs available in these employment areas
and normalize by the expected number of new households in 2030.

```{r}
#| label: calc-basic-buffer
#| cache: true

# constants
dist_bike <- 7.5 # bike distance in km
dist_ebike <- 15 # ebike distance in km

# buffer housing areas
gwl_bike_buffer <- st_buffer(gwl, dist = dist_bike * 1000)
gwl_ebike_buffer <- st_buffer(gwl, dist = dist_ebike * 1000)

# jobs per new resident

lisa_banen <- lisa |>
  select("BANEN") # heavy dataset, so first take only the needed column

jobs <- gwl_bike_buffer |>
  select(oid, ProjNAAM, TOT2030) |>
  st_join(lisa_banen) |>
  group_by(oid) |>
  summarise(
    TOT2030 = first(TOT2030),
    banen = sum(BANEN, na.rm = T),
    # banen_per_woning = banen / TOT2030,
    ProjNAAM = first(ProjNAAM)
  ) |>
  st_join(bevolking_pc6 |> select(aantal_woningen)) |>
  group_by(oid) |>
  summarise(
    ProjNAAM = first(ProjNAAM),
    nieuwe_woningen_2030 = first(TOT2030),
    banen = first(banen),
    bestaande_woningen = sum(aantal_woningen, na.rm = T),
    banen_per_nieuwe_woning = banen / nieuwe_woningen_2030,
    banen_per_totaal_woningen = banen / (bestaande_woningen + nieuwe_woningen_2030)
  )
```

Then, we can plot these.

:::{.column-page}
```{r}
#| label: fig-map-jobs-cycling-distance2
#| fig-cap: "Banen op < 7,5 km afstand van grootschalige woningbouwlocaties"
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Banen"
#|   - "Banen per nieuwe woning (2030)"
#|   - "Banen per totaal aantal woningen (inclusief bestaande en gepland)"
#| layout-ncol: 2

jobs_long <- jobs |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      banen,
      banen_per_nieuwe_woning,
      banen_per_totaal_woningen
    ),
    names_to = "group",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  arrange(group, value)

labels <- c(
  banen = "Banen",
  banen_per_nieuwe_woning = "Banen per nieuwe\nwoning (2030)",
  banen_per_totaal_woningen = "Banen per totaal aantal woningen\n(inclusief bestaande en gepland)"
)

palettes <- c(
  banen = "viridis",
  banen_per_nieuwe_woning = "cividis",
  banen_per_totaal_woningen = "inferno"
)

make_job_map <- function(data) {
  group <- unique(data$group)

  ggplot(data) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = value), color = NA, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_sf(data = nl_border, fill = NA) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(
      option = palettes[[group]],
      labels = scales::label_number()
    ) +
    labs(fill = labels[[group]]) +
    theme_void()
}

plots <- jobs_long |>
  group_split(group) |>
  map(make_job_map)

plots[[1]]
plots[[2]]
plots[[3]]
```
:::
